translations.title: Finding Area by Decomposing and Rearranging
translations.explanation: Finding Area by Decomposing and Rearranging is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Area and Surface Area”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.G.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and other shapes; apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Finding Area by Decomposing and Rearranging. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 4 and 3 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 4 × 3 = 12 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 6 and 7 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 6 × 7 = 42 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 4 and 3. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 12. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 6 and 7. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 42. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Finding Area by Decomposing and Rearranging. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Finding Area by Decomposing and Rearranging. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Bases and Heights of Parallelograms
translations.explanation: Bases and Heights of Parallelograms is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Area and Surface Area”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.EE.A.2, CCSS:6.G.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Write, read, and evaluate expressions in which letters stand for numbers. a. Write expressions that record operations with numbers and with letters standing for numbers. For example, express the calculation “Subtract y from 5” as 5 – y. Find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and other shapes; apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Bases and Heights of Parallelograms. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 5x + 2 = 17. Subtract 2 and divide by 5; the solution is x = 3. Example 2: Solve 4x + 7 = 19. Subtract 7 and divide by 4; the solution is x = 3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 2 from both sides to get 5x = 15. Step 2: divide both sides by 5. Step 3: x=3. Step 4: substitute: 5(3)+2=17, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 7 from both sides to get 4x = 12. Step 2: divide both sides by 4. Step 3: x=3. Step 4: substitute: 4(3)+7=19, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Bases and Heights of Parallelograms. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Bases and Heights of Parallelograms. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

Krok 1: odejmij 7 od obu stron: 4x = 12. Krok 2: podziel obie strony przez 4. Krok 3: x=3. Krok 4: sprawdzenie: 4(3)+7=19, więc równanie jest spełnione.

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń wykorzystuje własności działań i działania odwrotne do zapisywania, interpretowania, przekształcania i rozwiązywania wyrażeń, równań oraz nierówności. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Surface Pole of a Cube. Wyrażenie opisuje wartość, równanie stwierdza równość dwóch wyrażeń, a nierówność je porównuje. Przekształcenia równoważne zachowują zbiór rozwiązań. Podstawienie pozwala sprawdzić, czy dana wartość spełnia relację.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Rozwiąż 3x + 5 = 26. Odejmij 5 i podziel przez 3; otrzymujemy x = 7. Przykład 2: Rozwiąż 6x + 5 = 35. Odejmij 5 i podziel przez 6; otrzymujemy x = 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: odejmij 5 od obu stron: 3x = 21. Krok 2: podziel obie strony przez 3. Krok 3: x=7. Krok 4: sprawdzenie: 3(7)+5=26, więc równanie jest spełnione. Krok 1: odejmij 5 od obu stron: 6x = 30. Krok 2: podziel obie strony przez 6. Krok 3: x=5. Krok 4: sprawdzenie: 6(5)+5=35, więc równanie jest spełnione.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Surface Pole of a Cube. Nie wykonuj działania tylko po jednej stronie równania bez uzasadnienia. Redukuj wyłącznie wyrazy podobne. Przy mnożeniu nawiasu przez liczbę ujemną pomnóż każdy składnik w nawiasie.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Surface Pole of a Cube. Rozpoznaj strukturę algebraiczną, konsekwentnie zastosuj własności lub działania odwrotne, rozwiąż albo uprość i sprawdź wynik przez podstawienie lub inne równoważne sprawdzenie.

translations.title: Designing a Tent
translations.explanation: Designing a Tent is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Area and Surface Area”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.G.A.1, CCSS:6.G.A.4. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and other shapes; apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems. Represent three-dimensional figures using nets made up of rectangles and triangles, and use the nets to find the surface area of these figures. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Designing a Tent. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 3 and 5 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 3 × 5 = 15 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 7 and 5 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 7 × 5 = 35 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 3 and 5. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 15. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 7 and 5. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 35. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Designing a Tent. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Designing a Tent. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Introducing Ratios and Ratio Language
translations.explanation: Introducing Ratios and Ratio Language is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Introducing Ratios”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.RP.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities. For example, “The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every 2 wings there was 1 beak.” “For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes.” Instructional focus: Students compare quantities multiplicatively and use equivalent ratios, unit rates, tables, graphs, equations, and percentages to describe proportional relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Introducing Ratios and Ratio Language. A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. Equivalent ratios scale both quantities by the same nonzero factor. In y = kx, k is the constant of proportionality and equals the unit rate when the variables have the corresponding units.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The ratio 3:5 is equivalent to 9:15 because both terms were multiplied by 3. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 5/3 = 1.67. Example 2: The ratio 4:6 is equivalent to 12:18 because both terms were multiplied by 3. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 6/4 = 1.5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: preserve the order 3:5. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 3. Step 3: obtain 9:15. Step 4: divide 5 by 3 to obtain unit rate 1.67 and retain the contextual units. Step 1: preserve the order 4:6. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 3. Step 3: obtain 12:18. Step 4: divide 6 by 4 to obtain unit rate 1.5 and retain the contextual units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Introducing Ratios and Ratio Language. Do not compare ratios using only one component. Keep units and order consistent. A relationship with a nonzero intercept is not directly proportional, even if some pairs look almost proportional.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Introducing Ratios and Ratio Language. State the ratio with units and order, find an equivalent ratio or unit rate, represent the relationship, and check that both quantities scale consistently.

translations.title: Introducing Stosunki and Stosunek Language
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Introducing Stosunki and Stosunek Language” należy do działu „Introducing Ratios” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:6.RP.A.1. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń porównuje wielkości w sposób multiplikatywny i wykorzystuje równoważne stosunki, stawki jednostkowe, tabele, wykresy, równania oraz procenty do opisu proporcjonalności. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Introducing Stosunki and Stosunek Language. Stosunek porównuje dwie wielkości w ustalonej kolejności. Stosunki równoważne powstają przez pomnożenie obu wielkości przez ten sam niezerowy czynnik. W równaniu y = kx liczba k jest stałą proporcjonalności i odpowiada stawce jednostkowej.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Stosunek 3:5 jest równoważny 9:15, ponieważ obie liczby pomnożono przez 3. Druga wielkość na jedną jednostkę pierwszej wynosi 5/3 = 1.67. Przykład 2: Stosunek 4:6 jest równoważny 12:18, ponieważ obie liczby pomnożono przez 3. Druga wielkość na jedną jednostkę pierwszej wynosi 6/4 = 1.5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: zachowaj kolejność 3:5. Krok 2: pomnóż obie wielkości przez ten sam czynnik 3. Krok 3: otrzymaj 9:15. Krok 4: podziel 5 przez 3, aby otrzymać stawkę jednostkową 1.67, i zachowaj jednostki z kontekstu. Krok 1: zachowaj kolejność 4:6. Krok 2: pomnóż obie wielkości przez ten sam czynnik 3. Krok 3: otrzymaj 12:18. Krok 4: podziel 6 przez 4, aby otrzymać stawkę jednostkową 1.5, i zachowaj jednostki z kontekstu.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Introducing Stosunki and Stosunek Language. Nie porównuj stosunków na podstawie tylko jednej liczby. Zachowuj kolejność i jednostki. Zależność z niezerowym wyrazem wolnym nie jest proporcjonalnością prostą, nawet jeśli część punktów wygląda podobnie.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Introducing Stosunki and Stosunek Language. Zapisz stosunek z jednostkami i właściwą kolejnością, wyznacz równoważny stosunek lub stawkę jednostkową, przedstaw zależność i sprawdź zgodne skalowanie obu wielkości.

translations.title: Defining Equivalent Ratios
translations.explanation: Defining Equivalent Ratios is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Introducing Ratios”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.RP.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities. For example, “The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every 2 wings there was 1 beak.” “For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes.” Instructional focus: Students compare quantities multiplicatively and use equivalent ratios, unit rates, tables, graphs, equations, and percentages to describe proportional relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Defining Equivalent Ratios. A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. Equivalent ratios scale both quantities by the same nonzero factor. In y = kx, k is the constant of proportionality and equals the unit rate when the variables have the corresponding units.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The ratio 8:7 is equivalent to 40:35 because both terms were multiplied by 5. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 7/8 = 0.875. Example 2: The ratio 6:9 is equivalent to 24:36 because both terms were multiplied by 4. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 9/6 = 1.5.

Step 4: divide 7 by 8 to obtain unit rate 0.875 and retain the contextual units. Step 1: preserve the order 6:9. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 4. Step 3: obtain 24:36. Step 4: divide 9 by 6 to obtain unit rate 1.5 and retain the contextual units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Defining Equivalent Ratios. Do not compare ratios using only one component. Keep units and order consistent. A relationship with a nonzero intercept is not directly proportional, even if some pairs look almost proportional.

translations.title: How Many Groups? (Part 1)
translations.explanation: How Many Groups? (Part 1) is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Dividing Fractions”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.NS.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions, and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem. For example, create a story context for (2/3) ÷ (3/4) and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient; use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (2/3) ÷ (3/4) = 8/9 because 3/4 of 8/9 is 2/3. (In general, (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/bc.) How much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally? How many 3/4-cup servings are in 2/3 of a cup of yogurt? How wide is a rectangular strip of land with length 3/4 mi and area 1/2 square mi? Instructional focus: Students extend arithmetic to signed, rational, and irrational numbers and reason about magnitude, order, opposites, absolute value, and operations on the number line. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: How Many Groups? (Part 1). Position on the number line determines order. Opposites are the same distance from zero on different sides. Absolute value is distance from zero. Operation rules must be connected to direction, magnitude, or properties rather than memorized without meaning.

translations.title: Truth and Equations
translations.explanation: Truth and Equations is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Expressions and Equations”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.EE.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering a question: which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true? Use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Truth and Equations. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 5x + 2 = 22. Subtract 2 and divide by 5; the solution is x = 4. Example 2: Solve 6x + 3 = 45. Subtract 3 and divide by 6; the solution is x = 7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 2 from both sides to get 5x = 20. Step 2: divide both sides by 5. Step 3: x=4. Step 4: substitute: 5(4)+2=22, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 3 from both sides to get 6x = 42. Step 2: divide both sides by 6. Step 3: x=7. Step 4: substitute: 6(7)+3=45, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Truth and Equations. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Truth and Equations. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń wykorzystuje własności działań i działania odwrotne do zapisywania, interpretowania, przekształcania i rozwiązywania wyrażeń, równań oraz nierówności. translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Truth and Równania. Wyrażenie opisuje wartość, równanie stwierdza równość dwóch wyrażeń, a nierówność je porównuje. Przekształcenia równoważne zachowują zbiór rozwiązań. Podstawienie pozwala sprawdzić, czy dana wartość spełnia relację.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Rozwiąż 5x + 2 = 22. Odejmij 2 i podziel przez 5; otrzymujemy x = 4. Przykład 2: Rozwiąż 6x + 3 = 45. Odejmij 3 i podziel przez 6; otrzymujemy x = 7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: odejmij 2 od obu stron: 5x = 20. Krok 2: podziel obie strony przez 5. Krok 3: x=4. Krok 4: sprawdzenie: 5(4)+2=22, więc równanie jest spełnione. Krok 1: odejmij 3 od obu stron: 6x = 42. Krok 2: podziel obie strony przez 6. Krok 3: x=7. Krok 4: sprawdzenie: 6(7)+3=45, więc równanie jest spełnione.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Truth and Równania. Nie wykonuj działania tylko po jednej stronie równania bez uzasadnienia. Redukuj wyłącznie wyrazy podobne. Przy mnożeniu nawiasu przez liczbę ujemną pomnóż każdy składnik w nawiasie.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Truth and Równania. Rozpoznaj strukturę algebraiczną, konsekwentnie zastosuj własności lub działania odwrotne, rozwiąż albo uprość i sprawdź wynik przez podstawienie lub inne równoważne sprawdzenie.

translations.title: Practice Solving Equations and Representing Situations with Equations
translations.explanation: Practice Solving Equations and Representing Situations with Equations is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Expressions and Equations”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.EE.B.5, CCSS:6.EE.B.6, CCSS:6.EE.B.7, CCSS:6.NS.B.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering a question: which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true? Use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true. Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem; understand that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set. Solve real-world and mathematical problems by writing and solving equations of the form x + p = q and px = q for cases in which p, q and x are all nonnegative rational numbers. Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm for each operation. Instructional focus: Students use properties and inverse operations to write, interpret, transform, and solve numerical or algebraic expressions, equations, and inequalities. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Practice Solving Equations and Representing Situations with Equations. An expression represents a value; an equation states that two expressions are equal; an inequality compares values. Equivalent transformations preserve the solution set. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 3x + 2 = 11. Subtract 2 and divide by 3; the solution is x = 3. Example 2: Solve 3x + 4 = 19. Subtract 4 and divide by 3; the solution is x = 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 2 from both sides to get 3x = 9. Step 2: divide both sides by 3. Step 3: x=3. Step 4: substitute: 3(3)+2=11, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 4 from both sides to get 3x = 15. Step 2: divide both sides by 3. Step 3: x=5. Step 4: substitute: 3(5)+4=19, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Practice Solving Equations and Representing Situations with Equations. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Practice Solving Equations and Representing Situations with Equations. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

For example, in a problem involving motion at constant speed, list and graph ordered pairs of distances and times, and write the equation d = 65t to represent the relationship between distance and time. Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities. For example, “The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every 2 wings there was 1 beak.” “For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes.” Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems, e.g., by reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, or equations. a. Make tables of equivalent ratios relating quantities with whole-number measurements, find missing values in the tables, and plot the pairs of values on the coordinate plane. Use tables to compare ratios. b. Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed... Instructional focus: Students compare quantities multiplicatively and use equivalent ratios, unit rates, tables, graphs, equations, and percentages to describe proportional relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Two Related Quantities, Part 1. A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. Equivalent ratios scale both quantities by the same nonzero factor. In y = kx, k is the constant of proportionality and equals the unit rate when the variables have the corresponding units.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The ratio 7:10 is equivalent to 35:50 because both terms were multiplied by 5. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 10/7 = 1.43. Example 2: The ratio 4:5 is equivalent to 8:10 because both terms were multiplied by 2. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 5/4 = 1.25.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: preserve the order 7:10. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 5. Step 3: obtain 35:50. Step 4: divide 10 by 7 to obtain unit rate 1.43 and retain the contextual units. Step 1: preserve the order 4:5. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 2. Step 3: obtain 8:10. Step 4: divide 5 by 4 to obtain unit rate 1.25 and retain the contextual units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Two Related Quantities, Part 1. Do not compare ratios using only one component. Keep units and order consistent. A relationship with a nonzero intercept is not directly proportional, even if some pairs look almost proportional.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Two Related Quantities, Part 1. State the ratio with units and order, find an equivalent ratio or unit rate, represent the relationship, and check that both quantities scale consistently.

translations.title: Positive and Negative Numbers
translations.explanation: Positive and Negative Numbers is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Rational Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.NS.C.5, CCSS:6.NS.C.6. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand that positive and negative numbers are used together to describe quantities having opposite directions or values (e.g., temperature above/below zero, elevation above/below sea level, credits/debits, positive/negative electric charge); use positive and negative numbers to represent quantities in real-world contexts, explaining the meaning of 0 in each situation. Understand a rational number as a point on the number line. Extend number line diagrams and coordinate axes familiar from previous grades to represent points on the line and in the plane with negative number coordinates. a. Recognize opposite signs of numbers as indicating locations on opposite sides of 0 on the number line; recognize that the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself, e.g., –(–3) = 3, and that 0 is its own opposite. b. Understand signs of numbers in ordered pairs as indicating locations in quadrants of the coordinate plane; recognize that when two ordered pairs differ only by signs, the locations of the points are related by reflections across one or both axes. c. Find and position integers and other rational numbers on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram; find and position pairs of integers and other rational numbers on a coordinate plane. Instructional focus: Students extend arithmetic to signed, rational, and irrational numbers and reason about magnitude, order, opposites, absolute value, and operations on the number line. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Positive and Negative Numbers. Position on the number line determines order. Opposites are the same distance from zero on different sides. translations.title: Writing and Graphing Inequalities
translations.explanation: Writing and Graphing Inequalities is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Rational Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.EE.B.8, CCSS:6.NS.C.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Write an inequality of the form x > c or x < c to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem. Recognize that inequalities of the form x > c or x < c have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on number line diagrams. Understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers. a. Interpret statements of inequality as statements about the relative position of two numbers on a number line diagram. For example, interpret –3 > –7 as a statement that –3 is located to the right of –7 on a number line oriented from left to right. b. Write, interpret, and explain statements of order for rational numbers in real- world contexts. For example, write –3 oC > –7 oC to express the fact that –3 oC is warmer than –7 oC. c. Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from 0 on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation. For example, for an account balance of –30 dollars, write |–30| = 30 to describe the size of the debt in dollars. d. Distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order. For example, recognize that an account balance less than –30 dollars represents a debt greater than 30 dollars. translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Writing and Graphing Inequalities. Substitution provides a direct way to test whether a value satisfies a relation.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Solve 3x + 1 = 19. Subtract 1 and divide by 3; the solution is x = 6. Example 2: Solve 3x + 8 = 35. Subtract 8 and divide by 3; the solution is x = 9.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: subtract 1 from both sides to get 3x = 18. Step 2: divide both sides by 3. Step 3: x=6. Step 4: substitute: 3(6)+1=19, so the equation is satisfied. Step 1: subtract 8 from both sides to get 3x = 27. Step 2: divide both sides by 3. Step 3: x=9. Step 4: substitute: 3(9)+8=35, so the equation is satisfied.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Writing and Graphing Inequalities. Do not perform an operation on only one side of an equation unless the transformation is justified. Combine only like terms. When distributing a negative factor, apply it to every term inside the parentheses.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Writing and Graphing Inequalities. Identify the algebraic structure, apply properties or inverse operations consistently, solve or simplify, and verify by substitution or an equivalent check.

translations.explanation: Drawing on the Coordinate Plane is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Rational Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.G.A.3, CCSS:6.NS.C.8. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Draw polygons in the coordinate plane given coordinates for the vertices; use coordinates to find the length of a side joining points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems. Solve real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane. Include use of coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Drawing on the Coordinate Plane. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 6 and 5 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 6 × 5 = 30 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 9 and 5 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 9 × 5 = 45 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 6 and 5. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 30. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 9 and 5. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 45. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Drawing on the Coordinate Plane. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Drawing on the Coordinate Plane. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Statistical Questions
translations.explanation: Statistical Questions is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Data Sets and Distributions”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.SP.A.1, CCSS:6.SP.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers. For example, “How old am I?” is not a statistical question, but “How old are the students in my school?” is a statistical question because one anticipates variability in students’ ages. Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: a. Reporting the number of observations. b. Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement. c. Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered. d. Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered. Instructional focus: Students formulate statistical questions, summarize distributions, compare data, and use chance models to reason from variability rather than from isolated values. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Statistical Questions. Describe data with context, center, spread, shape, and unusual values as appropriate. Probability is between 0 and 1. Experimental results vary, so conclusions should distinguish observed data from what a model predicts.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For the data [10, 12, 14, 14, 16], the mean is (10 + 12 + 14 + 14 + 16)/5 = 13.2. The range is 16 - 10 = 6. Example 2: For the data [10, 12, 14, 14, 16], the mean is (10 + 12 + 14 + 14 + 16)/5 = 13.2. The range is 16 - 10 = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 66. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 13.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 10 from maximum 16 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context. Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 66. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 13.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 10 from maximum 16 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Statistical Questions. Do not report a statistic without saying what it represents. Do not assume a small sample must match the theoretical probability exactly. Check whether comparisons use the same scale and whether the sample supports the conclusion.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Statistical Questions. Connect the question to an appropriate representation or statistic, calculate carefully, describe variability, and make a conclusion that stays within the evidence.

The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm for each operation. Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: a. Reporting the number of observations. b. Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement. c. Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered. d. Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered. Instructional focus: Students extend arithmetic to signed, rational, and irrational numbers and reason about magnitude, order, opposites, absolute value, and operations on the number line. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Using Mean and MAD to Make Comparisons. Position on the number line determines order. Opposites are the same distance from zero on different sides. Absolute value is distance from zero. Operation rules must be connected to direction, magnitude, or properties rather than memorized without meaning.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Start at -12 on the number line and add 5. Moving 5 units to the right lands at -7, so -12 + 5 = -7. The absolute value |-12| = 12. Example 2: Start at -7 on the number line and add 4. Moving 4 units to the right lands at -3, so -7 + 4 = -3. The absolute value |-7| = 7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: locate -12. Step 2: addition of positive 5 means move right 5 units. Step 3: arrive at -7. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-12|=12 records distance from zero, not the sign. Step 1: locate -7. Step 2: addition of positive 4 means move right 4 units. Step 3: arrive at -3. Step 4: check magnitude and sign; |-7|=7 records distance from zero, not the sign.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Using Mean and MAD to Make Comparisons. Do not confuse a negative sign with an instruction to subtract. When comparing negative numbers, the number farther left is smaller. Keep exact values, such as radicals, when a decimal approximation is not required.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Using Mean and MAD to Make Comparisons. Represent the numbers on an appropriate scale, apply operation and order rules carefully, and check sign and magnitude before accepting the result.

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń rozszerza działania na liczby ze znakiem, wymierne i niewymierne oraz analizuje ich wielkość, porządek, liczby przeciwne, wartość bezwzględną i działania na osi liczbowej. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: System liczbowy — Using Mean and MAD to Make Comparisons. Położenie na osi liczbowej określa porządek. Liczby przeciwne leżą w tej samej odległości od zera po przeciwnych stronach. Wartość bezwzględna oznacza odległość od zera. Reguły działań warto wiązać z kierunkiem, wielkością i własnościami.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Zacznij w punkcie -12 na osi liczbowej i dodaj 5. Przesunięcie o 5 w prawo prowadzi do -7, więc -12 + 5 = -7. Wartość bezwzględna |-12| = 12. Przykład 2: Zacznij w punkcie -7 na osi liczbowej i dodaj 4. Przesunięcie o 4 w prawo prowadzi do -3, więc -7 + 4 = -3. Wartość bezwzględna |-7| = 7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: zaznacz -12. Krok 2: dodanie dodatniej liczby 5 oznacza ruch o 5 w prawo. Krok 3: otrzymujesz -7. Krok 4: sprawdź znak i wielkość; |-12|=12 oznacza odległość od zera. Krok 1: zaznacz -7. Krok 2: dodanie dodatniej liczby 4 oznacza ruch o 4 w prawo. Krok 3: otrzymujesz -3. Krok 4: sprawdź znak i wielkość; |-7|=7 oznacza odległość od zera.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: System liczbowy — Using Mean and MAD to Make Comparisons. Nie myl znaku liczby ujemnej z działaniem odejmowania. Przy porównywaniu liczb ujemnych liczba położona bardziej w lewo jest mniejsza. Zachowuj wartości dokładne, np. pierwiastki, jeśli przybliżenie dziesiętne nie jest potrzebne.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: System liczbowy — Using Mean and MAD to Make Comparisons. Przedstaw liczby na odpowiedniej skali, ostrożnie zastosuj reguły działań i porządku oraz sprawdź znak i wielkość wyniku.

translations.title: Median
translations.explanation: Median is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Data Sets and Distributions”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.SP.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: a. Reporting the number of observations. b. Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement. c. Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered. d. Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered. Instructional focus: Students formulate statistical questions, summarize distributions, compare data, and use chance models to reason from variability rather than from isolated values. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Median. Describe data with context, center, spread, shape, and unusual values as appropriate. Probability is between 0 and 1. Experimental results vary, so conclusions should distinguish observed data from what a model predicts.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For the data [4, 6, 8, 8, 10], the mean is (4 + 6 + 8 + 8 + 10)/5 = 7.2. The range is 10 - 4 = 6. Example 2: For the data [11, 13, 15, 15, 17], the mean is (11 + 13 + 15 + 15 + 17)/5 = 14.2. The range is 17 - 11 = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 36. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 7.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 4 from maximum 10 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context. Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 71. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 14.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 11 from maximum 17 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Median. Do not report a statistic without saying what it represents. Do not assume a small sample must match the theoretical probability exactly. Check whether comparisons use the same scale and whether the sample supports the conclusion.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Median. Connect the question to an appropriate representation or statistic, calculate carefully, describe variability, and make a conclusion that stays within the evidence.

translations.title: Using Data to Solve Problems
translations.explanation: Using Data to Solve Problems is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Data Sets and Distributions”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.SP.A.2, CCSS:6.SP.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand that a set of data collected to answer a statistical question has a distribution which can be described by its center, spread, and overall shape. Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by: a. Reporting the number of observations. b. Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement. c. Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered. d. Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered. Instructional focus: Students formulate statistical questions, summarize distributions, compare data, and use chance models to reason from variability rather than from isolated values. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Using Data to Solve Problems. Describe data with context, center, spread, shape, and unusual values as appropriate. Probability is between 0 and 1. Experimental results vary, so conclusions should distinguish observed data from what a model predicts.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: For the data [5, 7, 9, 9, 11], the mean is (5 + 7 + 9 + 9 + 11)/5 = 8.2. The range is 11 - 5 = 6. Example 2: For the data [6, 8, 10, 10, 12], the mean is (6 + 8 + 10 + 10 + 12)/5 = 9.2. The range is 12 - 6 = 6.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 41. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 8.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 5 from maximum 11 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context. Step 1: verify there are 5 observations. Step 2: add them to obtain 46. Step 3: divide by 5 to get mean 9.2. Step 4: subtract minimum 6 from maximum 12 to get range 6 and interpret both statistics in context.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Using Data to Solve Problems. Do not report a statistic without saying what it represents. Do not assume a small sample must match the theoretical probability exactly. Check whether comparisons use the same scale and whether the sample supports the conclusion.

translations.title: How Do We Choose?
translations.explanation: How Do We Choose? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting it All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:6.RP.A.1, CCSS:6.RP.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities. For example, “The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every 2 wings there was 1 beak.” “For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes.” Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems, e.g., by reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, or equations. a. Make tables of equivalent ratios relating quantities with whole-number measurements, find missing values in the tables, and plot the pairs of values on the coordinate plane. Use tables to compare ratios. b. Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed. For example, if it took 7 hours to mow 4 lawns, then at that rate, how many lawns could be mowed in 35 hours? At what rate were lawns being mowed? c. Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100 (e.g., 30% of a quantity means 30/100 times the quantity); solve problems involving finding the whole, given a part and the percent. d. Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units; manipulate and transform units appropriately when multiplying or dividing quantities. 1Expectations for unit rates in this grade are limited to non-complex fractions. Instructional focus: Students compare quantities multiplicatively and use equivalent ratios, unit rates, tables, graphs, equations, and percentages to describe proportional relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: How Do We Choose?. A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. Equivalent ratios scale both quantities by the same nonzero factor. In y = kx, k is the constant of proportionality and equals the unit rate when the variables have the corresponding units.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The ratio 7:7 is equivalent to 14:14 because both terms were multiplied by 2. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 7/7 = 1. Example 2: The ratio 6:4 is equivalent to 12:8 because both terms were multiplied by 2. The second quantity per one unit of the first is 4/6 = 0.667.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: preserve the order 7:7. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 2. Step 3: obtain 14:14. Step 4: divide 7 by 7 to obtain unit rate 1 and retain the contextual units. Step 1: preserve the order 6:4. Step 2: multiply both quantities by the same factor 2. Step 3: obtain 12:8. Step 4: divide 4 by 6 to obtain unit rate 0.667 and retain the contextual units.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: How Do We Choose?. Do not compare ratios using only one component. Keep units and order consistent. A relationship with a nonzero intercept is not directly proportional, even if some pairs look almost proportional.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: How Do We Choose?. State the ratio with units and order, find an equivalent ratio or unit rate, represent the relationship, and check that both quantities scale consistently.

translations.title: Stosunki i proporcjonalność — How Do We Choose?
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Stosunki i proporcjonalność — How Do We Choose?” należy do działu „Putting it All Together” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:6.RP.A.1, CCSS:6.RP.A.3. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń porównuje wielkości w sposób multiplikatywny i wykorzystuje równoważne stosunki, stawki jednostkowe, tabele, wykresy, równania oraz procenty do opisu proporcjonalności. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Stosunki i proporcjonalność — How Do We Choose?. Stosunek porównuje dwie wielkości w ustalonej kolejności. Stosunki równoważne powstają przez pomnożenie obu wielkości przez ten sam niezerowy czynnik. W równaniu y = kx liczba k jest stałą proporcjonalności i odpowiada stawce jednostkowej.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Stosunek 7:7 jest równoważny 14:14, ponieważ obie liczby pomnożono przez 2. Druga wielkość na jedną jednostkę pierwszej wynosi 7/7 = 1. Przykład 2: Stosunek 6:4 jest równoważny 12:8, ponieważ obie liczby pomnożono przez 2. Druga wielkość na jedną jednostkę pierwszej wynosi 4/6 = 0.667.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: zachowaj kolejność 7:7. Krok 2: pomnóż obie wielkości przez ten sam czynnik 2. Krok 3: otrzymaj 14:14. Krok 4: podziel 7 przez 7, aby otrzymać stawkę jednostkową 1, i zachowaj jednostki z kontekstu. Krok 1: zachowaj kolejność 6:4. Krok 2: pomnóż obie wielkości przez ten sam czynnik 2. Krok 3: otrzymaj 12:8. Krok 4: podziel 4 przez 6, aby otrzymać stawkę jednostkową 0.667, i zachowaj jednostki z kontekstu.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Stosunki i proporcjonalność — How Do We Choose?. Nie porównuj stosunków na podstawie tylko jednej liczby. Zachowuj kolejność i jednostki. Zależność z niezerowym wyrazem wolnym nie jest proporcjonalnością prostą, nawet jeśli część punktów wygląda podobnie.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Stosunki i proporcjonalność — How Do We Choose?. Zapisz stosunek z jednostkami i właściwą kolejnością, wyznacz równoważny stosunek lub stawkę jednostkową, przedstaw zależność i sprawdź zgodne skalowanie obu wielkości.
